ox: Wrong. Glucose plus fructose is sucrose (table sugar). Trap: sucrose is the most familiar disaccharide.
Correct. Lactose (milk sugar) is galactose joined to glucose by a beta-1,4 glycosidic bond. Lactase is the enzyme that splits it.
Wrong. Glucose plus glucose is maltose (alpha-1,4) or cellobiose (beta-1,4). Trap: assuming a disaccharide must be two identical sugars.
Wrong. Galactose plus fructose is not a common dietary disaccharide. Trap: combining the two sugars you did not use for sucrose.

p: A disaccharide is two single sugars (monosaccharides) joined by a glycosidic bond, a link made when water is removed.
Lactose is the sugar in milk. It is made of galactose and glucose. People who lack lactase cannot split it and get lactose intolerance.

q40.eli: Think of two LEGO bricks snapped together. Different brick pairs make different sugars: milk sugar is one galactose brick plus one glucose brick.
mem: Lactose = galactose + glucose (beta-1,4)
Sucrose = glucose + fructose
Maltose = glucose + glucose (alpha-1,4)
q40.mn: GaL-actose: Galactose + Glucose make Lactose. Both start with G, and the L in Lactose matches the L in Lactase, the enzyme that splits it.
q40.trap: Do not swap lactose and sucrose. Lactose has galactose; sucrose has fructose.

ox: Correct. Saturated chains have no double bonds, so they are straight and stack closely. More contact means more van der Waals (weak London) attractions, which take more heat to break, so the melting point is higher.
Wrong. Hydrocarbon tails have no O-H or N-H groups, so they do not hydrogen-bond. Trap: assuming a higher melting point always means hydrogen bonds.
Wrong. Both types have mostly nonpolar tails; polarity is not the difference. Trap: using polarity as a default answer.
Wrong. Saturated means no C=C double bonds. Unsaturated fats have them. Trap: reversing the definition.

concept.t: Fatty acid packing and melting point
p: Van der Waals forces are weak attractions between molecules that get stronger the more closely molecules touch. Saturated fatty acids have only single C-C bonds, so the chain is straight.
Unsaturated fatty acids have cis double bonds that put a kink in the chain. Kinked chains pack loosely, so they melt at lower temperatures.

q41.eli: Straight pencils stack tightly in a box. Bent pencils leave gaps and fall apart easily.
mem: Saturated = no C=C, straight, higher melting point (solid, like butter)
Unsaturated (cis) = kinked, lower melting point (liquid, like oil)
Longer chain = higher melting point
q41.trap: Do not say hydrogen bonds or polarity. It is about packing and van der Waals contact.

ox: Correct. SN2 is favored by a primary (unhindered) carbon, a strong nucleophile and a polar aprotic solvent. The nucleophile attacks from behind in one step, which inverts the stereocenter.
Wrong. Tertiary substrate with a polar protic solvent describes SN1. SN1 gives racemization, but the question asks for SN2.
Wrong. SN2 never keeps the configuration. The backside attack always flips it. The trap is saying 'any substrate'; crowded ones fail.
Wrong. A carbocation intermediate belongs to SN1. SN2 is concerted, so there is no intermediate.

p: SN2 means substitution, nucleophilic, bimolecular. The nucleophile attacks the carbon from the side opposite the leaving group, and the leaving group leaves at the same moment. There is only one step.
Because of the backside attack, the stereocenter flips (inversion). Crowded carbons block the attack, so methyl and primary work best.

q81.eli: It is like pushing someone off a seat by sliding in from the opposite side at the same moment. No one waits in between, and the seat faces the other way.
mem: SN2: methyl > 1° > 2° (3° does not work)
Strong nucleophile, polar aprotic solvent (DMSO, acetone)
One step, rate = k[substrate][Nu], inversion
q81.trap: Mixing up SN1 and SN2 features. Carbocation, 3°, protic solvent and racemization go with SN1.

ox: Correct. NaBH4 is a hydride (H-) source. The hydride adds to the carbonyl carbon, and the oxygen then picks up a proton. An aldehyde gives a primary alcohol.
Wrong. A secondary alcohol comes from reducing a ketone. An aldehyde carbon has only one carbon attached, so it becomes primary.
Wrong. A carboxylic acid is an oxidation product of an aldehyde. NaBH4 is a reducing agent, so the direction is wrong.
Wrong. An ester needs an alcohol and an acid derivative. Neither is present, and NaBH4 does not make esters.

p: NaBH4 (sodium borohydride) is a mild reducing agent. It delivers H- (hydride) to the carbon of a C=O group. The oxygen then gains an H and becomes an OH group.
Aldehydes become primary alcohols. Ketones become secondary alcohols. NaBH4 does not reduce esters or acids; LiAlH4 does.

ox: Correct. The amine nitrogen of one amino acid attacks the carboxyl carbon of another. Water is lost, so it is a condensation (dehydration) reaction, and an amide bond forms.
Wrong. Hydrolysis uses water to break the bond. It is the reverse reaction.
Wrong. Oxidizing two thiols (-SH) forms a disulfide bond between cysteines, not a peptide bond.
Wrong. A phosphodiester linkage joins nucleotides in DNA and RNA, not amino acids.

p: A peptide bond is the link between two amino acids. It forms when the -NH2 group of one amino acid joins the -COOH group of another. A molecule of water is released.
A reaction that joins two molecules and releases water is called a condensation (or dehydration synthesis). Breaking the bond adds water back, which is hydrolysis.

Wrong. Enantiomers are non-superimposable mirror images. A meso compound is superimposable on its own mirror image, so the inversion gives the same molecule.
Wrong. A racemic mixture is a 50:50 mix of two chiral enantiomers. This compound is achiral, so no such pair exists.
Wrong. Diastereomers are different compounds. Changing both centers of a meso compound gives the same compound, not a different one.

p: A stereocenter is a carbon with four different groups. A meso compound has stereocenters but is not chiral, because it has an internal mirror plane. Its mirror image is itself.
In 2,3-dibromobutane, both stereocenters hold the same set of groups. So the R,S form is the same as S,R. The R,R and S,S forms are the real enantiomer pair.

mem: Meso: stereocenters plus an internal mirror plane, so achiral

ox: Correct. In trans-1,2, one methyl points up and the other down on adjacent carbons. A chair can put both in equatorial positions, which is the roomy position.
Wrong. For cis-1,2 both groups point the same way, so on adjacent carbons one is axial and one is equatorial in either chair.
Wrong. For 1,3, the cis isomer is the diequatorial one. The trans isomer always has one axial group.
Wrong. For 1,4, the trans isomer is diequatorial. The cis isomer always has one axial group.

p: In a chair, each carbon has an axial position (straight up or down) and an equatorial position (out to the side). Equatorial is roomier, so large groups prefer it.
Rule of thumb: 1,2 and 1,4 substitution: trans can be diequatorial. 1,3 substitution: cis can be diequatorial.

mem: 1,2: trans = diequatorial
1,3: cis = diequatorial

Cis on 1,2 / 1,4 or trans on 1,3 always leaves one group axial

ox: Wrong. The two salts are not mirror images, so they are not enantiomers. Enantiomers would have identical solubilities and could not be separated.
Wrong. The amine does not change the acid's configuration. Racemization would not help separation anyway.
Correct. The (R)-amine pairs with R-acid to give (R,R) and with S-acid to give (S,R). These are not mirror images, so they are diastereomers with different solubilities. One crystallizes first.
Wrong. Both enantiomers of the acid react with the amine, forming two different salts. It is the salts that differ.

p: Enantiomers have identical physical properties, so you cannot separate them by crystallization. Diastereomers are stereoisomers that are not mirror images, and they do differ in solubility and melting point.
Reacting a racemic acid with a pure chiral amine gives two diastereomeric salts. Crystallize one out, then add strong acid to free the pure acid.

ox: Wrong. Meso compounds need two or more stereocenters with symmetry. This product has only one stereocenter, so it is chiral.

Correct. A tertiary halide in water reacts by SN1. The leaving group leaves first and gives a flat carbocation. Water can attack from either face, so both R and S alcohols form and the mixture is nearly racemic.
Wrong. Pure inversion is the SN2 outcome. A crowded tertiary carbon cannot be attacked from the back.
Wrong. Pure retention would need the carbocation to remember its shape. A flat cation does not, so both faces are open.

p: In SN1, the leaving group leaves first, making a carbocation. A carbocation carbon is sp2 and flat. The nucleophile (here water) can attack from either face.
Attack from both faces gives both enantiomers, so a chiral starting material gives a racemic or nearly racemic product. Tertiary carbons and polar protic solvents favor SN1.

x5D_027.eli: Picture a flat pancake you can flip from either side. After the flip you cannot tell which side was originally up.
mem: Tertiary + polar protic solvent + weak nucleophile: SN1
Planar carbocation gives racemization

ox: Wrong. I- is the best nucleophile in protic solvents, where small anions are caged by hydrogen bonds. In DMSO there is no such caging, so that order flips. This is the classic trap.
Correct. DMSO has no O-H or N-H to hydrogen bond to anions, so the anions are bare. Then nucleophilicity follows basicity, and F- is the strongest base of the halides.
Wrong. Cl- is a weaker base than F-, so in a non-hydrogen-bonding solvent it is less nucleophilic.
Wrong. Br- is a weaker base than F- and Cl-, so it ranks below them in aprotic solvents.

p: A polar protic solvent has O-H or N-H bonds (water, alcohols). It surrounds anions with hydrogen bonds, which hides small anions like F-. A polar aprotic solvent (DMSO, acetone) has no such bonds, so anions are free.
With free anions, a stronger base is a stronger nucleophile. So in aprotic solvents: F- > Cl- > Br- > I-. In protic solvents the order reverses.

x5D_029.eli: In water, F- is wrapped in a heavy blanket of water molecules and cannot move well. In DMSO it has no blanket, so it runs freely.
mem: Protic solvent: I- > Br- > Cl- > F-
Aprotic solvent: F- > Cl- > Br- > I-
Aprotic: nucleophilicity tracks basicity
x5D_029.trap: Using the protic-solvent order. Read the solvent first.

ox: Wrong. Carbonyls are very reactive electrophiles. Addition and substitution at C=O are everywhere in organic chemistry and biochemistry.
Wrong. The alpha-carbon is next to the carbonyl carbon. It becomes nucleophilic after deprotonation to an enolate. It is not the electrophile.
Wrong. The oxygen is electron-rich and reacts with electrophiles such as H+, not with nucleophiles. This reverses the polarity.
Correct. Oxygen is more electronegative and pulls electrons in the C=O bond toward itself. That leaves the carbon partly positive, so nucleophiles attack it.

p: A carbonyl is a carbon double-bonded to oxygen. Oxygen is more electronegative, meaning it pulls electrons harder. So oxygen is partly negative and carbon is partly positive.
A nucleophile is an electron-rich species that attacks positive centers. It therefore attacks the carbonyl carbon, and the pi electrons shift onto oxygen.

x5D_032.eli: Oxygen is like the strong kid in a tug-of-war who pulls the rope toward himself. The carbon side is left short of rope, so it attracts anyone who is giving.
mem: Carbonyl C: electrophilic (delta+)
Carbonyl O: nucleophilic/basic (delta-)
Alpha-carbon becomes nucleophilic as an enolate
x5D_032.trap: Mixing up which atom is positive. The less electronegative carbon is the one that is attacked.

ox: Wrong. This is direct capture of the secondary cation at C2. It misses that a more stable cation is available by a hydride shift, so it forms only in minor amounts.
Correct. Ionization gives a secondary cation at C2. A hydride shifts from C3 to C2, putting the charge on C3, which is tertiary and more stable. Water attacks C3 to give 2-methylbutan-2-ol.
Wrong. This would need OH on a terminal carbon. No cation or shift places the charge there.
Wrong. This needs a different skeleton. A methyl shift here would not give a more stable cation, and the carbon skeleton does not fit.

p: In SN1, a carbocation forms. More substituted carbocations are more stable: tertiary > secondary > primary. If a neighbor carbon can donate an H (hydride shift) or CH3 to make a more stable cation, it often does.
Water then attacks the new, more stable cation. So the OH ends up where the cation ended up, not where the leaving group was.

1,2-hydride and methyl shifts give more stable cations
The nucleophile attaches where the final cation sits

ox: Wrong. Azide is a good nucleophile. Rate not changing means azide is not in the rate-limiting step, not that it fails to react later.
Wrong. E2 is bimolecular, so its rate depends on the base. Tripling azide would triple the rate.
Correct. A rate unchanged by [N3-] means the nucleophile is not in the slow step. A tertiary chloride ionizes slowly to a carbocation, and azide attacks afterward. Rate = k[RCl].
Wrong. SN2 rate = k[RCl][Nu], so tripling Nu would triple the rate. A tertiary carbon is also too crowded for backside attack.

p: The rate law shows which species are in the slowest step. If doubling a reactant does nothing to the rate, that reactant is not in the slowest step. In SN1 the slow step is the leaving group departing, so only the substrate matters.
In SN2 and E2, both substrate and nucleophile/base appear in the rate law.

mem: SN1 rate = k[substrate], first order
SN2 and E2 rate depend on both substrate and Nu/base
Tertiary halide with no rate dependence on Nu: SN1

fm.f: Rate = k[RCl], where k = rate constant, [RCl] = concentration of the alkyl chloride (SN1 rate law)
fm.s: Rate = k[RCl], with no N3- term, so rate x 1 = same
fm.why: A reactant absent from the rate law cannot change the rate.
fm.nc: Just compare factors: no azide term, so the factor is 1.

ox: Correct. SN2 needs a backside approach to the C-Br carbon. The neighboring carbon holds three methyl groups. They physically block the nucleophile, so the reaction is extremely slow even though the carbon is primary.
Wrong. The alpha-carbon (the one holding Br) is CH2 and has two hydrogens. The problem is crowding next door, not missing hydrogens.
Wrong. Cation stability matters for SN1, not SN2. Also, this cation would be primary, which is very unstable.
Wrong. Bromide is a good leaving group, and similar primary bromides react quickly in SN2.

p: SN2 needs the nucleophile to reach the carbon from the side opposite the leaving group. Bulky groups near that carbon block the way. This is called steric hindrance.
The carbon next to the reacting one (the beta carbon) matters too. Neopentyl has a tert-butyl group there, so it is primary but behaves like a tertiary halide for SN2.

ox: Wrong. Sulfur is actually LESS electronegative than oxygen. The trap is thinking a polar C-S bond drives the reaction; the real driver is the positive charge on sulfur.

Correct. The methyl carbon has almost no crowding, so the nucleophile can reach it from behind. The sulfur carries a positive charge (sulfonium), so when it leaves as a neutral thioether it takes the bonding electrons easily.

concept.t: Why SAM is a methyl donor
p: SN2 means a nucleophile (electron-rich atom) attacks a carbon from the back while a leaving group (the piece that departs with the bonding electrons) leaves at the same time. It works best on carbons with few attached groups.

In SAM, the methyl is attached to a sulfur with a positive charge. That sulfur wants to leave as a neutral molecule, so it is a great leaving group. The methyl carbon is also small and open, so SAM is the cell's main methyl donor.

Wrong. Oxygen is electron-rich and holds the negative charge in resonance. It is not the electrophilic site.
Correct. Pushing the C=C electrons toward the oxygen leaves a partial positive charge on the beta carbon. Nucleophiles attack there (conjugate or 1,4 addition, such as the Michael reaction).
Wrong. The gamma carbon is not part of the conjugated C=C-C=O unit. It is not made electrophilic by it.

concept.t: Conjugated enones are electrophilic at beta
p: An alpha,beta-unsaturated ketone has a C=C right next to a C=O. Electrons can move through both double bonds (resonance), like water flowing along a pipe.
When they flow toward oxygen, the far end of the C=C, the beta carbon, loses electron density and becomes partly positive. Nucleophiles can attack it.

x5D_080.eli: Pulling one end of a rope makes the far end move too; the oxygen pulls and the beta carbon feels it.
mem: Two electrophilic sites: carbonyl carbon (1,2) and beta carbon (1,4).
Conjugate addition at the beta carbon is the Michael reaction.
The alpha carbon is not electrophilic in the enone.
x5D_080.trap: Alpha is the 'next to carbonyl' carbon, so it tempts students. Draw the resonance: the positive charge goes to beta.
x5D_080.academic: Written from standard MCAT content and independently fact-checked by a second AI reviewer. Not verified against AAMC 2025-26, Wikibooks, LibreTexts or Lehninger; expert review recommended.

ox: Correct. Cl- is an excellent leaving group (very weak base), and chlorine donates little resonance electron density to the carbonyl, so the carbon stays very electrophilic.
Wrong. Amides are the least reactive carboxylic acid derivatives. Nitrogen donates strongly by resonance and is a poor leaving group.
Wrong. Esters are less reactive. Alkoxide (RO-) is a poorer leaving group, and the oxygen donates resonance electrons into the carbonyl.
Wrong. Anhydrides are reactive, but a carboxylate is a poorer leaving group than chloride. They are second place, not first.

p: In nucleophilic acyl substitution, a nucleophile attacks the carbonyl carbon and a leaving group is kicked out. Two things speed this up: a more positive carbonyl carbon, and a better leaving group.
The better the leaving group (the weaker its basicity), the faster the reaction. Chloride is a very weak base, so acid chlorides are the most reactive.

x5D_086.eli: A door with a flimsy latch (chloride) opens at a light push; a door bolted shut (amide) barely moves.
mem: Order: acid chloride > anhydride > ester (and acid) > amide.
Better leaving group means more reactive.
More reactive derivatives can be made into less reactive ones, not the other way.
x5D_086.mn: Cl, An, Es, Am: 'Cats Always Eat Mice' (Chloride, Anhydride, Ester, Amide), most to least reactive.
x5D_086.trap: Anhydride looks very reactive, so it tempts students. Compare the leaving groups: chloride beats carboxylate.
x5D_086.academic: Written from standard MCAT content and independently fact-checked by a second AI reviewer. Not verified against AAMC 2025-26, Wikibooks, LibreTexts or Lehninger; expert review recommended.

ox: Wrong. The carbonyl oxygen comes from the carboxylic acid's C=O, which is unlabeled. The labeled alcohol oxygen does not end up there.
Wrong. The label is not scrambled. The alcohol's C-O bond is never broken, so the label stays in one place.
Wrong. The water leaves from the acid's OH, so it carries the acid's unlabeled oxygen. Students assume the alcohol loses its OH, but it only loses H.
Correct. The alcohol oxygen attacks the protonated carbonyl carbon and stays attached to its ethyl group. The acid loses its OH as water, so the 18O is in the ester's C-O-CH2CH3 oxygen.

p: Fischer esterification joins a carboxylic acid and an alcohol with an acid catalyst. The alcohol's oxygen acts as the nucleophile and attacks the carbonyl carbon.
After proton shuffling, the acid's OH leaves as water. So the acid loses OH and the alcohol loses only H. Labeling the alcohol oxygen proves this.

x5D_090.eli: Two train cars couple together: the alcohol car keeps its own connector (oxygen) and the acid car drops its connector (OH) as water.
mem: Acid loses OH; alcohol loses H.
Alcohol oxygen ends up in the ester's alkoxy position.
Water by-product has the acid's oxygen.
x5D_090.trap: Many assume water takes the alcohol's OH. Track the label with the nucleophile: it attacks and stays.
x5D_090.academic: Written from standard MCAT content and independently fact-checked by a second AI reviewer. Not verified against AAMC 2025-26, Wikibooks, LibreTexts or Lehninger; expert review recommended.

ox: Wrong. Esters can be re-formed from acids, for example by Fischer esterification in acid. Saponification is irreversible for a different reason.
Correct. The carboxylic acid formed is immediately deprotonated by base to a carboxylate. That resonance-stabilized anion is not electrophilic, so alkoxide cannot attack it to go backward.
Wrong. Evaporation is not the reason; the alcohol may be low-boiling or not. The driving force is the acid-base step.
Wrong. Hydroxide is a reactant that is used up (one full equivalent), not a catalyst.

p: Saponification means breaking an ester with hydroxide (OH-). Hydroxide attacks the carbonyl and an alkoxide leaves, giving a carboxylic acid.

In basic solution that acid loses its proton at once, becoming a carboxylate. The negative charge is spread over two oxygens, so it is very stable and cannot be attacked again. This final step pulls the reaction forward.

x5D_091.eli: It is like a one-way gate: once the product steps through (is deprotonated), it cannot walk back.
mem: Base hydrolysis of ester: irreversible, needs a full equivalent of OH-.
Product is a carboxylate salt plus an alcohol.
Acid hydrolysis of an ester is reversible.
x5D_091.trap: Calling hydroxide a catalyst is the common mistake. It is consumed.
x5D_091.academic: Written from standard MCAT content and independently fact-checked by a second AI reviewer. Not verified against AAMC 2025-26, Wikibooks, LibreTexts or Lehninger; expert review recommended.

ox: Wrong. Making the amide releases an H+ (as HCl); it does not need a proton. The extra amine is for the by-product.
Wrong. Amines are nucleophiles and bases here, not reducing agents. Nothing is being reduced.
Wrong. Only one amine ends up in the amide. A second addition would not give N-methylacetamide.
Correct. The reaction makes HCl. The second equivalent of amine soaks up that acid. Otherwise HCl protonates the amine, which then has no lone pair and cannot attack.

p: An amine attacks the acid chloride's carbonyl carbon, and chloride leaves. This gives the amide plus HCl.

HCl is a strong acid. It would turn amine into an ammonium ion (R-NH3+), which cannot act as a nucleophile because its lone pair is tied up. So you need a second base: another amine, or pyridine or triethylamine.

x5D_093.eli: The reaction makes a puddle of acid, and you need a sponge (the extra amine) to clean it up so the work can continue.
mem: Acid chloride + amine gives amide + HCl.
Use 2 equivalents of amine or add a base like pyridine.
Protonated amines are not nucleophilic.
x5D_093.trap: Do not think two amines bond to the carbon. The second one only acts as a base.
x5D_093.academic: Written from standard MCAT content and independently fact-checked by a second AI reviewer. Not verified against AAMC 2025-26, Wikibooks, LibreTexts or Lehninger; expert review recommended.

ox: Correct. The reaction is favorable (negative delta G), but amide resonance makes the C-N bond strong and the carbonyl weakly electrophilic. The activation energy is high, so it is very slow without a catalyst.
Wrong. Water can act as a nucleophile. It is just slow with amides without help.
Wrong. Peptide bonds are covalent amide bonds, not ionic.
Wrong. Hydrolysis is exergonic (negative delta G). Students mix up 'favorable' with 'fast'.

p: Delta G tells you whether a reaction CAN go downhill. Activation energy tells you how FAST it goes. They are separate ideas.

Peptide bonds are stabilized by resonance, so the barrier to breaking them is high. Hydrolysis is favorable but very slow until enzymes (proteases), strong acid, or heat lower the barrier. Catalysts do not change delta G.

x5D_094.eli: A ball sits in a bowl at the top of a hill: rolling down would be good, but the bowl rim holds it there until someone pushes.
mem: Negative delta G does not mean fast.
Catalysts lower activation energy, not delta G.
Amide resonance gives stability and a high barrier.
x5D_094.trap: Seeing 'persists' and thinking the reaction is unfavorable. Persisting is about speed, not energy.
x5D_094.academic: Written from standard MCAT content and independently fact-checked by a second AI reviewer. Not verified against AAMC 2025-26, Wikibooks, LibreTexts or Lehninger; expert review recommended.

ox: Wrong. A simple carboxylic acid has no second carbonyl, so there is nothing to take the electrons. It needs very harsh conditions.
Correct. A beta-keto acid has a ketone two carbons from the acid carbon. The ketone oxygen takes the acid hydrogen through a six-membered cyclic transition state as CO2 leaves, giving acetone here.
Wrong. Aryl acids are resistant to heat decarboxylation. The ring does not help the electrons move.
Wrong. This is a gamma-keto acid. The ketone is too far to form the six-membered ring, so it does not decarboxylate easily.

p: Decarboxylation means losing CO2 from a carboxylic acid. It is easy only when a carbonyl sits at the beta position (the carbon two away from the acid carbon).
The electrons move around a six-atom ring: the O-H hydrogen goes to the ketone oxygen, a C-C bond breaks, and CO2 leaves. An enol forms, then tautomerizes to a ketone.

x5D_095.eli: It is like a zipper that only opens when a helper holds the right spot; with the helper in the right place, the CO2 just pops off.
mem: Beta-keto acids (and malonic acids) lose CO2 on gentle heating.
Mechanism uses a cyclic six-membered transition state.
3-Oxobutanoic acid gives acetone + CO2.
x5D_095.sc: Count from the COOH carbon: if the next carbon (alpha) is followed by a C=O at carbon 3, it is a beta-keto acid and will decarboxylate.
x5D_095.trap: The 4-oxo acid looks similar, but the ketone is one carbon too far away.
x5D_095.academic: Written from standard MCAT content and independently fact-checked by a second AI reviewer. Not verified against AAMC 2025-26, Wikibooks, LibreTexts or Lehninger; expert review recommended.

ox: Wrong. Triethylamine's lone pair is localized and the alkyl groups push in electron density, so it is strongly basic.
Wrong. Ethylamine is a normal alkylamine; its conjugate acid has pKa about 10.7, so it is a good base.
Correct. The amide nitrogen's lone pair is delocalized into the carbonyl by resonance, so it is not available to take a proton. Amides are essentially nonbasic.
Wrong. Pyridine's lone pair is in an sp2 orbital outside the ring's pi system, so it can accept a proton. It is weakly basic (conjugate acid pKa about 5), still more basic than an amide.

p: A base needs a free lone pair to grab a proton. If the lone pair is tied up in resonance, it is less available and the nitrogen is less basic.
In an amide, the nitrogen lone pair is shared with the C=O. That makes the amide nitrogen essentially nonbasic. Alkylamines have free lone pairs and are the most basic.

x5D_101.eli: A hand that is already holding something cannot catch a ball; a free hand can.
mem: Alkylamines: strongly basic (pKa of conjugate acid about 10-11).
Pyridine: weakly basic (about 5).
Amides: essentially nonbasic.
x5D_101.trap: All four have nitrogen, so students guess pyridine. Ask whether the lone pair is free or delocalized.
x5D_101.academic: Written from standard MCAT content and independently fact-checked by a second AI reviewer. Not verified against AAMC 2025-26, Wikibooks, LibreTexts or Lehninger; expert review recommended.

ox: Correct. In pyrrole the nitrogen lone pair is in a p orbital and provides two of the six pi electrons of the aromatic ring. Protonating it would destroy aromaticity, so pyrrole resists. Pyridine's lone pair is separate and free.
Wrong. Pyrrole's nitrogen does have a lone pair. The point is that it is being used in the aromatic system.
Wrong. Pyridine is aromatic, with six pi electrons.
Wrong. Pyridine's nitrogen is sp2, and its lone pair lies in the ring plane.

p: Aromatic rings are extra stable when they have 6 pi electrons in a flat, cyclic, fully conjugated ring. Losing that stability costs a lot of energy.

In pyrrole, the nitrogen lone pair is needed to reach six pi electrons, so it cannot bind a proton. In pyridine, the carbons and the N=C bond already give six, and the lone pair sits to the side, free to take a proton.

x5D_104.eli: In pyrrole the nitrogen's electrons are part of the team and cannot leave; in pyridine they are a spare player on the bench.
mem: Pyridine: lone pair in sp2 orbital in the plane, basic.
Pyrrole: lone pair part of the aromatic sextet, nonbasic.
Aromatic needs 4n+2 pi electrons (Huckel).
x5D_104.trap: Saying 'pyrrole has no lone pair' is wrong. It has one, but it is already committed.
x5D_104.academic: Written from standard MCAT content and independently fact-checked by a second AI reviewer. Not verified against AAMC 2025-26, Wikibooks, LibreTexts or Lehninger; expert review recommended.

ox: Correct. Each ethyl group adds electron density to nitrogen, so the products are at least as nucleophilic as ammonia. They compete for the remaining bromoethane and keep reacting.
Wrong. C-N bonds do not rearrange. The mixture comes from repeated SN2 alkylation.
Wrong. Bromoethane is a primary halide and reacts by SN2, not SN1. A primary carbocation would be too unstable.
Wrong. Ammonia is a good nucleophile with a lone pair. It attacks first.

p: Ammonia attacks an alkyl halide in an SN2 reaction and becomes a primary amine. Alkyl groups donate electrons, so this new amine is as nucleophilic, or more, than ammonia.
So the new amine also attacks the alkyl halide, giving secondary, tertiary, and even quaternary ammonium salts. You cannot stop at one product by using one equivalent.

x5D_106.eli: Giving a kid one cookie makes the kid better at grabbing more cookies, so the cookies end up spread unevenly.
mem: Direct alkylation of NH3 gives mixtures (overalkylation).
Alkyl groups make N more nucleophilic.
Clean primary amines: Gabriel synthesis or reductive amination.
x5D_106.trap: Do not blame SN1 or rearrangements. The product being a better nucleophile is the reason.
x5D_106.academic: Written from standard MCAT content and independently fact-checked by a second AI reviewer. Not verified against AAMC 2025-26, Wikibooks, LibreTexts or Lehninger; expert review recommended.

ox: Wrong. Adding an electron makes a species more negative, so a cation cannot form by reduction.
Correct. One electron added to ubiquinone gives the semiquinone, a radical whose unpaired electron is spread over the ring and both oxygens by resonance.
Wrong. Ubiquinol (the fully reduced form) needs two electrons and two protons, so it is a two-electron product.
Wrong. A dianion requires two electrons added, which is not a one-electron step.

p: Ubiquinone (coenzyme Q) can exist in three forms: oxidized quinone, the half-reduced semiquinone radical, and the fully reduced ubiquinol.

Each electron added is one step. One electron gives the semiquinone (a radical has an unpaired electron). Two electrons plus two H+ give ubiquinol. This lets Q link two-electron carriers like NADH with one-electron carriers like cytochromes.

x5D_114.eli: Climbing a ladder one rung at a time: one rung is the semiquinone, two rungs is ubiquinol.
mem: Q (oxidized) to QH. (semiquinone) to QH2 (ubiquinol).
Semiquinone is a stable radical intermediate.
Q carries electrons in the electron transport chain.
x5D_114.trap: Picking ubiquinol because it is the 'reduced form' ignores the one-electron wording.
x5D_114.academic: Written from standard MCAT content and independently fact-checked by a second AI reviewer. Not verified against AAMC 2025-26, Wikibooks, LibreTexts or Lehninger; expert review recommended.

ox: Wrong. The ring is not attacked at random. The OH group pushes electrons into only certain carbons, so the product is mostly one pattern. The trap is thinking a very reactive ring is also unselective.
Wrong. Ipso means the carbon that already holds the OH. Bromine replaces a ring hydrogen, not the OH group. The trap is picturing OH as a leaving group like in substitution at sp3 carbon.
Correct. The oxygen lone pair donates into the ring by resonance. This puts extra negative charge on the ortho and para carbons, so Br+ attacks there.
Wrong. Meta direction belongs to electron-withdrawing groups such as NO2 or C=O. OH is an electron donor. The trap is mixing up the two groups of directors.

p: A benzene ring is electron-rich and attacks electrophiles (electron-poor species like Br+). This is called electrophilic aromatic substitution. A group already on the ring can speed this up (activate) or slow it down (deactivate).

An OH group has a lone pair on oxygen that can flow into the ring (resonance). That adds negative charge at the ortho (next to) and para (opposite) carbons. Attack at those spots gives a more stable intermediate, so those products form.

x5D_116.eli: Think of the ring as a pond and OH as a tap pouring extra water onto the two spots right beside it and the one straight across. Visitors (Br+) go where the water is.
mem: Donors with lone pairs (OH, NH2, OR) activate and direct ortho/para.
Withdrawing groups (NO2, C=O, CN) deactivate and direct meta.
Halogens are the exception: deactivating but ortho/para.
x5D_116.trap: Do not say OH directs meta or that the OH itself is replaced. Lone-pair donors send groups ortho and para.
x5D_116.academic: Written from standard MCAT content and independently fact-checked by a second AI reviewer. Not verified against AAMC 2025-26, Wikibooks, LibreTexts or Lehninger; expert review recommended.

ox: Wrong. C1 and C2 are neighbors. Bonding C1 oxygen to C2 would give a tiny strained ring of three atoms. The trap is picking the groups that sit closest on paper.
Wrong. Fructose is a ketose, so it has no aldehyde. C1 is a CH2OH group. The trap is borrowing glucose, which has an aldehyde at C1, and its pyranose ring.
Correct. The C5 OH attacks the C2 ketone carbon. The ring has C2, C3, C4, C5 and the oxygen, which is five atoms, so it is a furanose (a hemiketal).
Wrong. The C4 OH attacking C2 would make a ring of only four atoms (C2, C3, C4, O), which is too strained. The trap is miscounting the ring size.

p: Sugars in water mostly exist as rings. A ring forms when one of the sugar's own OH groups attacks its carbonyl carbon (the C=O). The product is a hemiketal if the carbonyl was a ketone, or a hemiacetal if it was an aldehyde.
Fructose is a ketose: its carbonyl is at C2. If the C5 OH attacks, the ring has 5 atoms (furanose). If the C6 OH attacks, the ring has 6 atoms (pyranose).

x5D_124.eli: It is like bending a chain until one end clips onto a link near the other end. A chain bent into a small loop of five links is a furanose.
mem: Fructose: ketone at C2, so a ketose.
C5 OH attack gives five-membered furanose; C6 OH gives six-membered pyranose.
Ring atoms = carbons from carbonyl to attacking OH, plus the ring oxygen.
x5D_124.sc: Count ring atoms: carbons from the carbonyl to the attacking OH carbon, plus one oxygen. C2 to C5 is 4 carbons plus O = 5.
x5D_124.trap: Fructose has no aldehyde and the C1 and C4 OH groups cannot make stable rings. Count ring size.
x5D_124.academic: Written from standard MCAT content and independently fact-checked by a second AI reviewer. Not verified against AAMC 2025-26, Wikibooks, LibreTexts or Lehninger; expert review recommended.

ox: Wrong. Omega-6 would mean the last double bond starts at C12 (18 - 12 = 6). Here there is one more double bond at C15. The trap is stopping at the second double bond.
Wrong. 9 is the first delta position, counted from the carboxyl end. Omega counts from the methyl end. The trap is mixing the two numbering systems.
Correct. The last double bond starts at C15. Omega = 18 - 15 = 3, so this is an omega-3 fatty acid (alpha-linolenic acid).
Wrong. Delta 15 is a position counted from the carboxyl end, not an omega class. The trap is copying a delta number straight into omega.

p: Fatty acids are long carbon chains with a carboxyl group (COOH) at one end and a methyl group (CH3) at the other. Delta (Δ) numbers count from the carboxyl carbon, which is C1. Omega (ω) counts from the methyl end.
The omega class tells you how far the double bond nearest the methyl end is from that end. For an 18-carbon chain, omega = 18 minus the starting position of the last double bond.

x5D_144.eli: Two people count houses on a street from opposite ends. Delta counts from the front door of the street; omega counts from the dead end.
mem: Delta counts from COOH; omega counts from CH3.
Omega = chain length - last double bond position.
Alpha-linolenic acid is omega-3; linoleic acid is omega-6.

fm.f: omega = N - d, where N = number of carbons in the chain, d = start position of the double bond nearest the methyl end (delta number), omega = what we solve for
fm.why: The distance from the methyl end to the last double bond defines the omega class.

x5D_144.trap: Do not read a delta number as omega. Subtract the last double bond position from the chain length.
x5D_144.academic: Written from standard MCAT content and independently fact-checked by a second AI reviewer. Not verified against AAMC 2025-26, Wikibooks, LibreTexts or Lehninger; expert review recommended.

ox: Wrong. Phospholipids have only two fatty acids, and PLA2 removes just one. Three fatty acids belong to triacylglycerols. The trap is confusing phospholipids with fats.
Wrong. Phosphatidic acid plus free choline comes from phospholipase D, which cuts after the phosphate. The trap is mixing up the lettered enzymes.
Correct. PLA2 cuts the ester at the sn-2 carbon of glycerol. This frees a fatty acid (often arachidonic acid) and leaves a one-tailed lysophospholipid.
Wrong. Diacylglycerol plus a phosphorylated head group is made by phospholipase C. The trap is the same lettered-enzyme mix-up.

p: A phospholipid has a glycerol backbone, two fatty acid tails, and a phosphate head group. Phospholipases are enzymes that cut specific bonds in it. The letter tells you which bond.
PLA1 and PLA2 cut off a tail at C1 or C2. PLC cuts just before the phosphate. PLD cuts just after it.

x5D_147.eli: Picture a toy with two tails and a head attached to a middle block. Each enzyme is scissors that cuts at one specific joint.
mem: PLA2 releases the sn-2 fatty acid (often arachidonic acid) and leaves a lysophospholipid.
PLC gives diacylglycerol plus a phosphorylated head (e.g., IP3).
PLD gives phosphatidic acid plus free head group (e.g., choline).
x5D_147.trap: The lettered enzymes are easy to swap. A2 means a fatty acid comes off at carbon 2.
x5D_147.academic: Written from standard MCAT content and independently fact-checked by a second AI reviewer. Not verified against AAMC 2025-26, Wikibooks, LibreTexts or Lehninger; expert review recommended.

ox: Wrong. Soaps are charged (carboxylate salts) and form micelles very well. The trap is thinking charge blocks self-assembly.

Correct. A one-tailed soap has a wide head and a thin tail, a cone shape, so it packs into a sphere (micelle). A two-tailed phospholipid is about as wide at the tails as at the head, a cylinder, so it packs into flat bilayers.
Wrong. A soap has a polar carboxylate head. Without it, it would not be amphipathic. The trap is overlooking the charged group.
Wrong. Phospholipids are classic amphipathic molecules: polar head, nonpolar tails. The trap is thinking only single-tailed molecules are amphipathic.

p: Amphipathic molecules have a water-loving (polar) head and a water-fearing (nonpolar) tail. In water, tails hide together and heads face the water.
The shape sets the structure. Cone-shaped molecules curve into spheres called micelles. Cylinder-shaped molecules stack into flat sheets called bilayers.

x5D_148.eli: Ice-cream cones fit in a ring around a point, like a ball. Soup cans stack side by side in flat rows.
mem: One tail: cone shape, micelle.
Two tails: cylinder shape, bilayer.
Both are amphipathic.
x5D_148.trap: Both molecules are amphipathic. The difference is shape, not charge or polarity.
x5D_148.academic: Written from standard MCAT content and independently fact-checked by a second AI reviewer. Not verified against AAMC 2025-26, Wikibooks, LibreTexts or Lehninger; expert review recommended.

ox: Wrong. L-cysteine has the same 3D arrangement as other L-amino acids. Only the label changes. The trap is assuming R and D, or S and L, always match.
Wrong. Disulfide bonds form between side-chain sulfurs. The alpha carbon is not touched. The trap is blaming a redox reaction for a naming rule.
Correct. In CH2SH, the first atom is carbon but it carries S, which beats the O atoms on the COOH carbon. So CH2SH outranks COOH, the priority order changes, and the label becomes R.
Wrong. The alpha carbon has four different groups (NH2, COOH, CH2SH, H), so it is a stereocenter. The trap is thinking the sulfur removes chirality.

p: D and L compare a molecule's shape with glyceraldehyde. R and S come from the CIP rules: rank the four groups by atomic number at the first point of difference, then look at the order from the highest to lowest.

For most amino acids the rank is NH2 > COOH > R > H, which makes L equal S. In cysteine the CH2SH carbon holds a sulfur (atomic number 16), which beats oxygen (8), so R outranks COOH and the label flips to R.

x5D_150.eli: Two kids can stand in the same line shape but be called by different names when ranked by a different rule. The line did not change; only the ranking rule did.
mem: Most L-amino acids are S; L-cysteine is R.
Sulfur outranks oxygen (16 vs 8).
D/L is geometry; R/S is priority.
x5D_150.trap: R/S and D/L are different systems. A flipped priority changes the label, not the structure.

ox: Wrong. Averaging all three pKa values has no meaning. Only the two values around the neutral form are averaged. The trap is averaging everything.
Wrong. This averages the carboxyl (2.2) and side chain (10.5) values, which do not flank the neutral form. The trap is picking the highest and lowest values.
Wrong. This averages the two alpha groups and ignores the basic side chain. That works for neutral amino acids, not lysine. The trap is using the simple formula.
Correct. Charge goes +2, +1, 0, -1. The neutral form sits between pKa 9.0 and 10.5, so pI = (9.0 + 10.5)/2 = 9.75.

concept.t: Isoelectric point of a basic amino acid
p: The isoelectric point (pI) is the pH where the molecule has no net charge. To find it, track the charge as pH rises and groups lose protons.
Lysine starts at +2 at low pH, becomes +1, then 0, then -1. The neutral form lies between the two pKa values that surround it. Average those two.

x5D_152.eli: Walk up a staircase of charges. You want the landing marked zero, and its middle lies between the two steps on either side.
mem: Basic amino acids (K, R, H) have pI above 7; acidic ones (D, E) below 7.
pI = average of the two pKa values that flank the zero-charge form.
Basic: average the two highest pKa values.

fm.f: pI = (pKa_a + pKa_b)/2, where pKa_a and pKa_b are the pKa values on each side of the neutral form, pI = what we solve for
fm.why: The neutral form exists only between those two pKa values.

x5D_152.sc: Basic residue: pI must be above 7, so pick the high answer. Only 9.75 qualifies.
x5D_152.trap: Averaging the two alpha-group pKa values (5.6) ignores the basic side chain.

ox: Correct. pH - pKa = 1, so [neutral]/[protonated] = 10/1. The protonated fraction is 1/(10+1) = 1/11, about 9%.
Wrong. 1% would need the pH to be two units above the pKa (ratio 100:1). The trap is miscounting the difference.
Wrong. This flips the ratio. Above the pKa the group is mostly deprotonated. The trap is forgetting which form dominates.
Wrong. 50% occurs only when pH equals pKa. Here pH is one unit higher. The trap is assuming pKa 6 means half at pH 7.

p: pKa is the pH at which half of a group is protonated and half deprotonated. When pH is above the pKa, the group is mostly deprotonated. When pH is below, it is mostly protonated.
Each one-unit difference changes the ratio ten-fold. The equation is pH = pKa + log([deprotonated]/[protonated]).

x5D_160.eli: It is like a seesaw balanced at pKa. Each pH unit above tips it ten times toward the deprotonated side.
mem: pH = pKa: 50% protonated.
pH one unit above pKa: 10:1 deprotonated, about 9% protonated.
pH one unit below pKa: about 91% protonated.

fm.f: pH = pKa + log([A-]/[HA]), where [A-] = deprotonated form, [HA] = protonated form, pKa = 6.0 here
fm.why: The difference between pH and pKa gives the ratio of the two forms.

x5D_160.sc: One unit above pKa: about 10% still protonated. Two units: about 1%.
x5D_160.trap: Flipping the ratio gives 91%. Above the pKa, the deprotonated form dominates.

ox: Correct. The imine carbon is flat. Cyanide can attack from the top or bottom face equally, so both enantiomers form in equal amounts: a racemic mixture.
Wrong. Only an enzyme or chiral catalyst would favor L. None are used here. The trap is assuming natural amino acids always come out L.
Wrong. Meso compounds need two or more stereocenters and an internal mirror plane. This product has one stereocenter. The trap is confusing racemic with meso.
Wrong. Nothing in the reagents favors D, just as nothing favors L. The trap is thinking a reaction must prefer one.

p: The Strecker synthesis makes an amino acid from an aldehyde, NH3 and HCN. The aldehyde and NH3 form an imine (C=N). Cyanide adds to the imine carbon, then hydrolysis turns the nitrile into a COOH group.
The imine carbon is flat (sp2). A new stereocenter formed by attack on a flat carbon, using achiral reagents, comes out as a 50:50 mix of both mirror images, called racemic.

x5D_161.eli: Flip a fair coin: heads and tails come up equally unless something biases it. An achiral reagent is a fair coin.
mem: Achiral reagents plus a flat carbon give a racemic product.
Racemic means 50:50 of the enantiomers.
Only enzymes or chiral catalysts give a single enantiomer.
x5D_161.trap: Lab synthesis without a chiral influence cannot give pure L. Cells use enzymes; flasks do not.

ox: Wrong. The adenine base is unchanged during hydrolysis. No energy is released from it. The trap is thinking the base is the battery.
Wrong. Breaking bonds always costs energy. ATP hydrolysis is favorable because the products are more stable, not because breaking is releasing. The trap is a common bond-energy misconception.
Wrong. Hydrolysis breaks an anhydride bond and does not form a new one. The trap is reading hydrolysis backward.
Correct. The three phosphates all carry negative charge and repel each other. Splitting off one phosphate relieves this strain. The products are also better resonance-stabilized and hydrated.

p: ATP has three phosphate groups in a row, each carrying negative charge. Like charges push each other apart, so the molecule is under strain.

When the terminal phosphoanhydride bond is hydrolyzed (split with water), ADP and inorganic phosphate (Pi) form. They repel less, have more resonance forms, and are better surrounded by water. This makes the reaction strongly exergonic (releases free energy).

x5D_173.eli: Three magnets forced together with the same sides touching are tense. Let one go and the others relax.
mem: ATP to ADP + Pi: about -30.5 kJ/mol.
Reasons: less charge repulsion, more resonance, better solvation.
Bond breaking itself costs energy; it is not the source.
x5D_173.trap: Do not say the energy is in the bond. 'High-energy bond' means the products are much more stable.

ox: Correct. Because DNA normally has thymine, any uracil in DNA must be damage from cytosine deamination. Uracil-DNA glycosylase can remove it safely.
Wrong. Thymine does not change how cytosine reacts. Cytosine still deaminates. The trap is thinking thymine protects other bases.
Wrong. Thymine has no amino group to lose, but that does not explain repair of cytosine damage. The trap is a true fact that does not answer the question.
Wrong. Uracil pairs with adenine, which causes a G-C to A-T mutation if unrepaired. The trap is reversing the pairing.

p: Cytosine can lose its amino group (deamination) and turn into uracil. If DNA used uracil normally, the cell could not tell a real U from a damaged C.
DNA uses thymine, which is uracil with a methyl group. So any U in DNA is an error. Uracil-DNA glycosylase removes it and repair enzymes fix the gap.

x5D_174.eli: If every paper in a pile is blue, a red one stands out and you can remove it. If red papers were normal, you could not tell the mistake.
mem: Thymine = 5-methyluracil.
Cytosine deamination gives uracil.
Uracil-DNA glycosylase removes U from DNA.
Unrepaired U pairs with A.
x5D_174.trap: The point is recognition, not prevention. Thymine makes damage detectable.

ox: Wrong. Grignard reagents do not reduce alcohols to alkanes. The trap is confusing a Grignard with a hydride reducing agent.
Wrong. The ester still reacts. The OH is a problem because it destroys the reagent, not the ester. The trap is thinking the OH deactivates the electrophile.
Wrong. Intramolecular reaction is not the main issue. The acid-base reaction is far faster. The trap is picking a nucleophile story when acid-base chemistry comes first.
Correct. A Grignard is a very strong base. The alcohol O-H (pKa about 16) protonates it instantly, making methane and wasting the reagent. A silyl ether removes the acidic proton.

p: A Grignard reagent (R-MgBr) acts like a carbanion, a carbon with a negative charge. It is a strong nucleophile and also a very strong base.
Any acidic proton, such as O-H, N-H, or a carboxylic acid, will protonate it first. To avoid that, the OH is temporarily converted to a silyl ether (protecting group). Later, fluoride removes it.

x5D_180.eli: If you try to paint a wall while someone keeps spilling water on your paint, it is ruined before it touches the wall. Cover the spill first.
mem: Grignards react with acidic protons before anything else.
Protect alcohols as silyl ethers (e.g., TBS).
Remove silyl groups with fluoride (e.g., TBAF).
x5D_180.trap: Acid-base chemistry is faster than addition. Check for acidic protons before using a Grignard.

ox: Wrong. Bromine is less electronegative than F and Cl, so its protons are less deshielded (about 2.7 ppm). The trap is thinking larger atoms deshield more.
Correct. Fluorine is the most electronegative halogen. It pulls electron density from the CH3 protons the most, so they are least shielded and appear farthest downfield (about 4.3 ppm).
Wrong. Chlorine is less electronegative than fluorine, so CH3Cl is at about 3.1 ppm. The trap is picking a familiar halogen.
Wrong. Iodine is the least electronegative, giving the most upfield signal (about 2.2 ppm). The trap is thinking the largest halogen has the biggest effect.

p: In 1H NMR, the chemical shift (in ppm) tells where a proton's signal appears. Downfield means higher ppm. Electrons near a proton shield it, shifting it upfield.
An electronegative atom pulls electrons away, which reduces shielding (deshielding), so the signal moves downfield. More electronegative neighbor means larger shift.

x5D_187.eli: Electrons are a blanket over the proton. A strong puller (fluorine) yanks the blanket off, so the proton feels the cold the most.
mem: More electronegative neighbor means more downfield.
CH3F > CH3Cl > CH3Br > CH3I in shift.
Size does not matter; electronegativity does.
x5D_187.sc: Electronegativity order F > Cl > Br > I equals the downfield order.
x5D_187.trap: Do not pick by atom size. Electronegativity controls deshielding.
